title: The Federation Offensive: From 70% to 49% in Weeks
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), autumn 1995 operations
content:
The military map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, largely frozen since late 1992, was redrawn in a matter of weeks during September and October 1995. A coordinated ground offensive by Croatian, HVO, and ARBiH forces — operating simultaneously with NATO's air campaign against VRS infrastructure — reduced Bosnian Serb-held territory from approximately 70 percent of Bosnia-Herzegovina to roughly 49 percent. The speed and scale of the territorial shift was without precedent in the war.

The offensive built on momentum generated by Operation Storm in early August, when the Croatian Army overran the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia in a matter of days. Croatian forces did not stop at the international border. Elements of the HV, operating alongside HVO units, pushed into western Bosnia in what became Operation Maestral, launched in early September. The offensive swept through the Livanjsko Polje and drove into the Bosanska Krajina, capturing territory that the VRS had held since the opening months of the war.

Simultaneously, ARBiH forces launched operations across multiple fronts. The 5th Corps, which had endured years of siege in the Bihac pocket, broke out and advanced eastward. In central Bosnia, ARBiH units pushed toward the Vrbas valley. Operation Sana, a combined HVO-ARBiH effort, drove toward the strategic towns of Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Mrkonjic Grad. Town after town that had been ethnically cleansed of its Bosniak and Croat populations in 1992 fell back to Federation control.

The VRS, which had appeared militarily dominant as recently as July when it overran Srebrenica and Zepa, proved unable to defend its vastly overextended front lines. Three years of siege warfare had consumed ammunition and manpower without building the mobile reserves needed to respond to a fast-moving conventional offensive. NATO air strikes had degraded command networks, destroyed ammunition depots, and shattered the logistical spine that connected VRS formations. The Rapid Reaction Force on Mount Igman had neutralized the heavy weapons ringing Sarajevo. Bosnian Serb units that had spent years in static positions found themselves outmaneuvered by forces that had spent those same years learning to fight with less.

The ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) documented the collapse of VRS positions in western Bosnia, noting how the territorial losses of September-October 1995 reversed gains that had been achieved through campaigns of persecution and forced displacement in 1992.

The offensive was not without its own darkness. The advance through the Krajina produced a new wave of displacement, this time of Serb civilians fleeing before Croatian and Bosniak forces. Homes were burned. Atrocities occurred. The cycle of ethnic expulsion that had defined the war did not pause because its direction had reversed.

By mid-October, when ceasefire negotiations gained traction, the front lines had settled into a rough approximation of the 51-49 percent territorial split that the Contact Group had proposed over a year earlier — a division that diplomats had failed to impose at the negotiating table but that military force had now inscribed on the ground. Whether this outcome reflected strategic design or fortunate coincidence remains debated. What is certain is that the territorial ratio achieved by force of arms became the foundation on which the Dayton Agreement was built.
